q.t: Find the HCF of 12 and 18.
q.e: 12 = 2² × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3². The common primes, each with its smaller power: 2 × 3 = 6.

q.t: Find the LCM of 12 and 18.
q.e: Take every prime with its larger power: 2² × 3² = 36 — the smallest number both divide into.

q.t: 140 = 2 × 2 × 5 × 7. How many prime factors does 140 have, counting repeats?
q.e: Each of 2, 2, 5, 7 is a prime factor; the 2 appears twice, so 4 in all.

q.t: By Euclid’s division lemma, 75 = 8 × 9 + r. Find r.
q.e: 8 × 9 = 72, and 75 − 72 = 3. The remainder must be less than the divisor 8, and it is.

q.t: Which of these is irrational?
q.e: 5 is not a perfect square, so √5 cannot be written as p/q. √16 = 4, and 0.75 and 22/7 are already fractions.

q.t: Find HCF × LCM of 8 and 14.
q.e: For two numbers, HCF × LCM always equals their product: 8 × 14 = 112 (HCF 2, LCM 56).

q.t: What kind of decimal is 13/40?
o: It cannot be written as a decimal
q.e: A fraction in lowest terms terminates when its denominator has only 2s and 5s as prime factors — then it can be turned into a power of 10.

q.t: ‘Every composite number can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way (apart from order).’ This is called…
q.e: It is the ‘fundamental’ fact about whole numbers: primes are the building blocks, and each number has one recipe.

q.t: Find the HCF of any two consecutive natural numbers, such as 20 and 21.
q.e: Any common factor would also divide their difference, which is 1 — so the only common factor is 1.

q.t: Write 7/8 as a decimal.
q.e: 8 = 2³, so multiply top and bottom by 5³ = 125: 875/1000 = 0.875.

q.t: Use Euclid’s division algorithm to find the HCF of 455 and 42.
q.e: 455 = 42 × 10 + 35, 42 = 35 × 1 + 7, 35 = 7 × 5 + 0. The last non-zero remainder, 7, is the HCF.

q.t: Find the LCM of 96 and 404.
The HCF of two numbers is 9 and their LCM is 459. One number is 27. Find the other.
q.e: HCF × LCM = product of the numbers, so the other is 9 × 459 ÷ 27 = 153.

q.t: Find the LCM of 6, 72 and 120.
43/(2⁴ × 5³) is a terminating decimal. After how many decimal places does it end?
q.e: Multiply top and bottom by 5 to get 2⁴ × 5⁴ = 10⁴ underneath — four decimal places.

q.t: Which of these has a non-terminating repeating decimal expansion?
q.e: 343 = 7³. A denominator with any prime other than 2 or 5 can never become a power of 10, so the decimal repeats forever.

q.t: Can 6ⁿ end with the digit 0 for some natural number n?
q.e: Ending in 0 means divisible by 10 = 2 × 5. 6ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 3ⁿ has no 5, and prime factorisation is unique, so a 5 can never appear.

q.t: Find the largest number that divides 245 and 1029 leaving remainder 5 each time.
q.e: Take the remainder away first: the number must divide 240 and 1024 exactly. HCF(240, 1024) = 16.

q.t: Find the smallest number which leaves remainder 4 when divided by 15, 20 and 24.
q.e: LCM(15, 20, 24) = 120 is divisible by all three; adding 4 leaves remainder 4 each time.
If it were rational, then √5 = (that number − 3)/2 would be rational too — but √5 is irrational.

q.t: Find the largest number that divides 1251, 9377 and 15628 leaving remainders 1, 2 and 3.
q.e: Subtract the remainders: it must divide 1250, 9375 and 15625 exactly. Their HCF is 5⁴ = 625.

q.t: Three bells ring at intervals of 9, 12 and 15 minutes. They ring together now. After how many minutes will they next ring together?
q.e: They ring together at a common multiple of 9, 12 and 15; the first one is LCM = 2² × 3² × 5 = 180.

q.t: Two tankers hold 850 L and 680 L of oil. What is the largest container that can measure both exactly?
q.e: The container size must divide both amounts, and we want the largest: HCF(850, 680) = 170.

q.t: Find the HCF of 2³ × 3² × 5 and 2² × 3³ × 7.
q.e: Take only primes common to both, each with its smaller power: 2² × 3² = 36.

q.t: When any odd positive integer is divided by 4, the remainder can only be…
q.e: Every integer is 4q, 4q + 1, 4q + 2 or 4q + 3. 4q and 4q + 2 are even, so an odd number must be 4q + 1 or 4q + 3.

q.t: 1/7 = 0.142857142857… How many digits are in its repeating block?
q.e: The block 142857 repeats. Dividing by 7 can leave only remainders 1–6, so the pattern repeats within 6 steps.

q.t: Write 0.363636… as a fraction in lowest terms.

q.e: LCM = product ÷ HCF = 306 × 657 ÷ 9 = 22338.

q.t: The product of two numbers is 1080 and their HCF is 30. Find their LCM.
q.e: Product = HCF × LCM, so LCM = 1080 ÷ 30 = 36.

q.t: Which of these is rational?
q.e: (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b², so it is 3 − 4 = −1. The others still contain √3.

q.t: A shop stacks 144 cartons of mango juice and 90 cartons of lemon juice. Each stack has the same number of cartons and only one kind of juice. What is the least number of stacks?
q.e: Fewest stacks means the biggest stack: HCF(144, 90) = 18. Then 144/18 + 90/18 = 8 + 5 = 13 stacks.

q.t: Find the smallest number which leaves remainders 8 and 12 when divided by 28 and 32.
q.e: 28 − 8 = 20 and 32 − 12 = 20: the number is 20 short of a common multiple. LCM(28, 32) − 20 = 224 − 20 = 204.

q.t: Sonia takes 18 minutes and Ravi 12 minutes to go once round a track. They start together from the same point in the same direction. After how many minutes are they together at the start again?
q.e: Each is at the start only at multiples of their own time, so both are there at LCM(18, 12) = 36.

q.t: Find the least number which leaves remainder 5 when divided by 6, 15 and 18.
q.e: LCM(6, 15, 18) = 90 is exactly divisible by all three; adding 5 leaves remainder 5: 95.

q.t: Write 0.2454545… (45 repeating) as a fraction in lowest terms.
Find the largest number that divides 2053 and 967 leaving remainders 5 and 7.
q.e: It must divide 2053 − 5 = 2048 and 967 − 7 = 960 exactly. HCF(2048, 960) = 64.

q.t: If n is an odd positive integer, n² − 1 is always divisible by…
q.e: n² − 1 = (n − 1)(n + 1): two consecutive even numbers, one of which is a multiple of 4 — so 2 × 4 = 8 divides it. (For n = 3 it is 8, so 16 cannot be forced.)

q.t: HCF(65, 117) can be written as 65m − 117. Find m.
The LCM of two numbers is 14 times their HCF, and LCM + HCF = 600. One number is 280. Find the other.
q.e: 15 × HCF = 600, so HCF = 40 and LCM = 560. Other number = 40 × 560 ÷ 280 = 80.

q.t: Which of these is irrational?
q.e: (2 − √3)² = 7 − 4√3, which still has √3. The others are 1, (3√2)² = 18 and √36 = 6.
